h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to classify settings as strong, weak, neutral or harmful, and to identify which settings can disconnect other parts from the outcome. Propose hypotheses only of two kinds. Self-conditioning: the edit's effect depends on the value it replaces, being more negative when that value is strong and more positive when it is empty or harmful. Disconnection: when the edited part cannot influence the outcome, its effect shrinks toward zero, so the direction is lower if the edit usually helps and higher if it usually hurts. Directions refer to the signed effect. For each hypothesis, state the edit's usual sign and a one-sentence mechanism. Cover varied edit fields and values. The critic should replace any hypothesis with an uncertain usual sign, competing effects or reliance on partial redundancy.

hyps.why: Replacing an empty 2->3 edge both adds a strong conv and reconnects node 2 to the output, so the gain is largest.
With edge 0 none, node 1 carries only zeros, so a conv on 1->2 has nothing to transform and its gain collapses.
When node 1 receives no input, edge 1->3 cannot contribute, so the conv's benefit vanishes.
With edge 2->3 removed, node 2 has no route to the output, so a conv on 0->2 cannot affect accuracy.
When node 2 is disconnected from the output, edge 1->3 becomes the cell's main deep path, so adding a conv there matters much more.
Removing the input-to-output residual shortcut costs most when the op being replaced is the crucial skip_connect rather than a weak op.
Replacing an empty 0->1 edge adds a strong conv and reactivates node 1 along with edges 2 and 4, maximizing the gain.
Swapping a strong 3x3 conv on the final serial edge for parameter-free pooling loses the most capacity.
Replacing a strong conv on edge 0->2 with pooling is a larger loss than replacing none or skip_connect.
A learnable 1x1 conv gains most when it replaces harmful smoothing pooling rather than an already useful op.
